title: The 2024 deepfake CFO fraud, read closely
body_md:
## What the public record says

The faces on the video call looked and sounded like company executives, and none of them could hear the employee. The call was a recording. That detail is easy to lose in retellings, and it comes from the Hong Kong government’s own reply of 26 June 2024, in which police described a case reported at the end of January. A fraudster emailed a staff member in the name of the chief financial officer (CFO) at the company’s UK head office and invited them to a group video conference about confidential transactions. The conference was **prerecorded**, police said, built from publicly available video and voice material, so there was no real-time exchange with the executives it showed. When the recording ended, the fraudster carried on with the payment instructions by instant message. The staff member authorized transfers totaling about **HK$200 million** to five local bank accounts. When the reply was written, the case was still under investigation.

Arup later said publicly that it was the company. In a 2025 interview, its CIO, Rob Greig, called the episode technology-enhanced social engineering and said the company’s systems and data were not compromised. That is Arup’s account of its own investigation; it doesn’t mean every incident of this kind leaves systems untouched. The government account does not say how payments were approved inside the company, exactly how the video was made, or what was finally recovered. Retellings that describe a fully interactive deepfake meeting, or insist that one callback would certainly have stopped everything at once, claim more than the record supports.

### What the faces could and couldn’t do

The email supplied authority and a reason for secrecy. The video supplied familiar faces and voices. Being a recording, it couldn’t answer questions, but the switch to instant messages kept the request moving. The money left at the moment a payment was authorized. That was the decision that mattered, and the ability to spot a flicker in a fake face weighed very little beside it. A face on a screen is not a signature, which is why a visual “deepfake test” makes a brittle safeguard. Some fakes look imperfect, and ordinary compression or a poor connection distorts genuine video too. Neither observation settles who is on the other end.

### A payment process that doesn’t hinge on a face

Treat what you see and hear as evidence of a claim, and authenticate the payment instruction itself through the process you already have. An organization can require that unusual transfers, new recipients and changes to bank details be checked through a previously recorded contact and the normal approval workflow. The approver reaches a known colleague or supplier on their own, records which transaction was confirmed, and brings in a second authorized person when policy requires it. A callback helps only if the number didn’t come from the suspicious request and the other channel isn’t controlled by the same party. A secret code spoken inside the same compromised meeting is weak. If a transfer has already gone out, contact the bank promptly and keep the request; reversal is not guaranteed.

A real executive may genuinely ask for a confidential, urgent transaction. Confidentiality changes who is told, not whether payment controls apply. A sound process lets the employee say, “I’ll confirm this through our standard route,” without a public accusation and without needing personal courage.

widget_config.goal: Separate what the record shows about the 2024 CFO impersonation case from what people assume, and insist on independent payment authorization even when the video looks familiar.
widget_config.today_action: Pick one payment or high-impact approval process and name the existing contact and second approver you would use if an urgent change arrived.
widget_config.scope: The real case took place in Hong Kong in January 2024 and is drawn from a 26 June 2024 government reply and a 2025 interview with Arup’s CIO. The reply said the investigation was still under way. The acquisition case and the practice scenario are invented.

sources.title: Hong Kong Government: LCQ9 on deepfake fraud
sources.scope: Official account dated 26 June 2024; the January case was still under investigation.

sources.title: World Economic Forum interview with Arup CIO Rob Greig
sources.scope: Direct interview published 4 February 2025; it gives Arup’s account, not a technical reconstruction.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US law-enforcement overview; the idea of verifying a payment applies anywhere.

sources.title: NCSC: How to spot a scam email, text message or call
sources.scope: UK consumer guidance, published 2021 and reviewed 2022; the habit of checking independently applies anywhere.

blocks.title: The Hong Kong case, as documented
blocks.situation: A real case, not a simulation: the 26 June 2024 Hong Kong government reply describes a January phishing email, a prerecorded fake video conference, follow-up instant messages and about HK$200 million sent to five accounts.
blocks.analysis: This is a narrow, official account of a payment being redirected. It does not prove a fully live, interactive deepfake, and it does not reveal the company’s internal approval controls. Arup’s CIO later confirmed the company had been deceived; the government reply says the case was still under police investigation.

blocks.title: A confidential payment that is real
blocks.situation: A CFO asks the finance team to prepare an urgent payment for an acquisition. The request is in the company’s usual payment system, a known executive confirms it on a number saved long before, and two authorized approvers sign as policy demands.
blocks.analysis: A request can be legitimate even when it is unusual and confidential. The existing approval route and an independent contact validate the instruction, with no reliance on a video image. The team should record the confirmation while keeping the deal details restricted.

blocks.title: Approve the transfer, or pause it
blocks.setup: You work in the finance team of an invented firm. A private video meeting asks you to make an urgent payment to a new supplier. No real bank details or payments are involved.

steps.prompt: On the video, someone who looks and sounds like your CFO asks you to pay a new payee. What matters first?

choices.text: Spot the new payee and treat this as a payment-change request that needs the normal controls.
choices.consequence: You have found the decision that carries the risk.
choices.explanation: A face and a voice don’t authorize new banking details.

choices.text: Approve it, because the face and voice match.
choices.consequence: The money may go to the wrong party.
choices.explanation: Familiar footage can be fabricated or replayed.

steps.prompt: The meeting insists the deal is secret and you must not consult your team. What do you say?

choices.text: Set the policy aside to keep the secret.
choices.consequence: One pressured decision now controls the money.
choices.explanation: Secrecy is no substitute for approval.

choices.text: Use the confidential approval route and bring in the required second approver.
choices.consequence: The deal stays restricted and the controls stay on.

steps.prompt: A chat message gives you a mobile number for a quick callback. Which number do you use?

choices.text: The executive’s number already in the company directory.
choices.consequence: The requester doesn’t get to choose how you confirm.
choices.explanation: A number supplied in the request can lead straight to the impostor.

choices.consequence: The fraudster may be the one who answers.
choices.explanation: A different channel isn’t independent if the contact came from the same claim.

steps.prompt: Whichever number you used, a colleague in finance now reaches the executive through the company directory. The executive denies making any such request. A transfer may be pending or may already have gone out. What now?

choices.text: Ask the person on the video to turn their head, and if the picture holds up, let the payment run.
choices.consequence: A pending payment may go through, or a completed one may never be reported.
choices.explanation: A look at the picture can’t overrule an independent denial, and it is no substitute for incident response.

choices.text: Halt any pending payment, alert the finance and security teams, call the bank at once if money has left, and keep the messages as policy requires.
choices.consequence: The team can contain what is still pending and ask the bank about anything already sent; recovery is not certain.
choices.explanation: An independent denial calls for containment whether or not the money has moved.

blocks.debrief: Replay the chain: apparent authority, familiar video, secrecy, new payee. The place to stop is the established payment approval plus a contact that is truly independent, not a do-it-yourself test of the picture.

blocks.title: Sticking to what the record says

questions.prompt: What did the Hong Kong government’s 2024 account say about the video conference?

choices.text: It was a fully interactive, live fake meeting.
choices.explanation: The official reply says nothing of the kind.

choices.text: It was prerecorded, and later instructions moved to instant messaging.
choices.explanation: The reply explicitly separates the recording from live interaction.

questions.prompt: A genuine executive asks for an urgent, confidential transfer. What is still needed?

choices.text: The firm’s own confidential checks and approval steps.
choices.explanation: The urgency and secrecy may be real, but neither authenticates a new payee.

choices.text: Immediate payment, since the executive is visible on video.
choices.explanation: Appearing on video is not payment authorization.

questions.prompt: You phone the number printed in the suspicious chat and someone answers. What does that prove?

choices.text: That you have reached the real CFO.
choices.explanation: The channel changed, but the source of the contact did not.

choices.text: Little: the requester may control that number.
choices.explanation: Independent verification needs a trusted contact that existed beforehand.

questions.prompt: What can you conclude about the investigation’s outcome from the June 2024 government reply?

choices.text: It was still ongoing on that date; the reply gives no final outcome.
choices.explanation: The source is dated, and it covers only what was known then.
The reply states no such thing.
